record.title: A shared-inference cost study finds allocation rules shift tenant bills by 12–14 points
record.summary: The paper introduces unalloc, which joins Kubernetes OpenCost allocations, LiteLLM gateway logs and OpenAI/Anthropic provider cost data to expose unattributed spend and reconcile it against invoices. Its accounting examples include synthetic billing fixtures: in one constructed deployment, owner labels only on leader pods left 66% of GPU spend unowned, while a fallback assigned 61% to a Helm chart label. Separately, a paper-reported H100/vLLM test found that token-based allocation assigned a retrieval-heavy tenant 12–14 percentage points more of a shared bill than equal time-share allocation across tested loads. The authors say neither meter is a ground truth; the repository describes one model and one two-minute run per load. These results show that labels, source overlap and allocation rules can change reported cost ownership, not that they change total compute expense or establish a uniquely correct cost split.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The paper and its public repository describe unalloc, a tool that joins OpenCost, LiteLLM, OpenAI and Anthropic cost data into a normalized ledger with owner attribution and invoice reconciliation. This establishes the published tool and method, not that every ledger total is correct for an arbitrary deployment.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In a constructed one-month OpenCost deployment scenario using synthetic allocations, the authors report that labeling only LeaderWorkerSet leader pods left 66% of a deployment’s GPU bill unowned; a fallback assigned 61% to a Helm chart name and reduced the displayed unallocated share to 4%. These are synthetic case-study values, not observed customer billing.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In the paper’s H100/vLLM test, a token meter assigned a retrieval-heavy tenant 12–14 percentage points more of the shared inference bill than equal time-share allocation across tested loads. The authors state that neither rule is ground truth. The repository describes one model and one two-minute run per load.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper reports that combining overlapping gateway and provider billing sources can double-count spend, and that reading only one page of a billing API can omit a large share. The repository warns that source overlap and pagination must be checked for each deployment.

evidence_gaps.description: The metering disagreement has been reported for one H100/vLLM setup and does not establish which allocation rule best represents resource responsibility or transfers across other servers and workloads.
The label-coverage example uses synthetic OpenCost allocations; no independently audited organization ledger or actual finance outcome was inspected.
The tool warns that gateway and provider sources may overlap and double-count, but how to identify overlap depends on organization-specific traffic routing.

brief.importance_rationale: If these failure modes recur in deployed shared inference, mismatched labels and metering choices can materially change team-level AI cost reports and downstream engineering or procurement decisions. A 4 reflects a meaningful accounting and system-design issue; the reported cases do not establish a general allocation standard, production savings or a uniquely true meter.
limitations: The paper is a single-author, non-peer-reviewed preprint; all case-study outcomes are author-reported and were not independently reproduced in this activation.
The 66% unowned and 61% fallback figures come from a constructed one-month synthetic OpenCost scenario, not observed customer spend.
The token-versus-time-share result is from one H100 running vLLM, with one model and one two-minute run per load according to the public repository.
Neither token count nor equal time-share is a ground truth for assigning shared GPU cost; alternative rules can allocate the same fixed bill differently.
Combining OpenCost, gateway and provider billing feeds can double-count overlapping charges; the correct source subset depends on an organization’s actual coverage.
Attribution disagreement does not demonstrate higher or lower total compute cost, realized savings or better product economics.
The claimed failure modes and measurement differences have not been tested across multiple providers, GPU types, models, serving stacks or production organizations.
brief.summary: The paper introduces unalloc, which joins Kubernetes OpenCost allocations, LiteLLM gateway logs and OpenAI/Anthropic provider cost data to expose unattributed spend and reconcile it against invoices. Its accounting examples include synthetic billing fixtures: in one constructed deployment, owner labels only on leader pods left 66% of GPU spend unowned, while a fallback assigned 61% to a Helm chart label. Separately, a paper-reported H100/vLLM test found that token-based allocation assigned a retrieval-heavy tenant 12–14 percentage points more of a shared bill than equal time-share allocation across tested loads. The authors say neither meter is a ground truth; the repository describes one model and one two-minute run per load. technical.claimed_result: Authors report synthetic allocation failures and, on an H100/vLLM setup, a 12–14 percentage-point difference between token and equal-time allocation for one retrieval-heavy tenant.
technical.demonstrated_result: The public repository and paper provide code, case-study fixtures and a described H100 validation run. The reported cost-allocation outcomes are not independent evidence of a universal meter or production savings.
technical.implementation_status: Public Apache-2.0 repository includes CLI source, tests, case-study artifacts and reproduction commands. Version 0.3.0 adds retained-input provenance and verification; the paper describes 0.2.3. This activation did not run the artifact.
technical.mechanism: unalloc normalizes cost rows from OpenCost, LiteLLM, OpenAI and Anthropic; users select a label dimension and optional fallback keys to calculate unattributed and fallback-attributed spend. The paper compares different allocation meters in shared inference and shows how duplicated or paginated sources can distort ledgers.
technical.regime: One H100 running vLLM, one model and one two-minute run per load for the GPU validation; separate synthetic/real-or-simulated case studies cover allocation and source integration. The authors warn that source overlap and workload-specific labels affect totals.
technical.reproducibility: Repository includes code, tests, case studies and commands to regenerate reports; the paper’s repository notes that byte-level input provenance proves identity, not that allocation is correct. No independent run was performed here.
technical.strongest_baseline: The paper contrasts token-based allocation with equal time-share and references Shapley-style energy attribution; it explicitly rejects treating either tested meter as a ground truth.

brief.title: A shared-inference cost study finds allocation rules shift tenant bills by 12–14 points
brief.why_it_matters: As organizations share inference servers across teams and products, cost attribution can influence product unit economics, budgets and make-versus-buy decisions. The study makes the accounting boundary visible: attribution depends on owner labels, provider-source overlap and the chosen allocation rule. Its evidence is a combination of synthetic ledgers and a narrow one-H100 experiment; it does not demonstrate customer savings or identify a uniquely correct tenant bill.
